items.title: 1996 spelling reform
items.claim: A German spelling reform was agreed in 1996 and implemented in stages. Which change is genuinely part of it?

options.text: Abolition of capital letters on nouns
Replacing ß with ss after short vowels in many words (e.g. dass instead of daß)

items.reveal:
The reform rationalised ss usage according to vowel length, modified some compound spellings and changed comma rules.

Major newspapers reversed and re-adopted parts of the reform in the early 2000s, settling on a revised version by 2006.
items.why: Orthographic reforms often face strong public reaction and partial reversal.

items.title: When the Duden first appeared
items.claim: Konrad Duden's first orthographic dictionary was published in which year?
items.reveal:
Duden's Vollstandiges Orthographisches Worterbuch der deutschen Sprache appeared in Leipzig in 1880.

A standard Orthographische Konferenz in 1901 made it the de facto national reference, a role it has held since.
items.why: Standardisation of writing systems was a late 19th-century project across Europe.

items.title: Swiss German diglossia
items.claim: German-speaking Switzerland uses Swiss German dialects for everyday speech and Standard German for which contexts?

options.text: Most writing, school instruction and formal broadcasting; daily speech remains dialect

items.reveal:
Linguists describe Swiss German as a textbook case of diglossia. Standard German is used for most written and formal contexts; dialect dominates speech, including on regional television.

Swiss German varieties differ substantially from one canton to another.
items.why: A community can run two registers of a language indefinitely in parallel.
